key_points.statement: Alfred Packer entered the Colorado mountains with five men in winter 1874 and emerged alone two months later looking well-nourished.
Packer offered contradictory accounts regarding how his companions died and how he acquired their personal possessions and money.
Physical evidence from the crime scene and coroner findings contradicted Packer's claims of self-defense and gradual starvation.
Packer avoided original murder charges due to a legal technicality regarding Colorado's territorial laws, ultimately receiving a manslaughter conviction.
Public perception and legal outcomes shifted over time, influenced by media campaigns and mixed modern forensic findings.

tensions.description: Packer claimed he killed Shannon Bell in self-defense after Bell murdered the others, whereas the coroner's report indicated all five men died from blunt force trauma to the head while sleeping.

Modern forensic studies found defensive wounds suggesting intentional violence, yet the discovery of a revolver matching bullet fragments in Bell's hip supports aspects of Packer's self-defense statement.
